NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang introduces 4 tiny Microduck robots during the NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026 keynote, demonstrating the future of physical artificial intelligence and robotics. Watch these miniature walking robots perform somersaults, follow commands, and even make unexpected mistakes during a memorable live demonstration. During the October 21, 2026 keynote in Berlin, Germany, Jensen Huang showcased Microduck robots developed through a collaboration involving Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face. Standing approximately 10 inches tall, these small bipedal robots demonstrate how artificial intelligence can be used to train machines to walk, balance, and perform complex physical movements. One of the highlights came when Huang asked the 4 robots to take a nap. While 3 immediately toppled over, the fourth needed additional prompting. Another Microduck even faced the wrong direction, adding some unexpected humor to the demonstration. Behind these entertaining moments is advanced robotics technology powered by NVIDIA's artificial intelligence ecosystem. Using NVIDIA Isaac Sim, Isaac Lab, and the Newton physics engine, developers can train virtual robots through thousands of simulated experiences before transferring learned behaviors to physical machines. The demonstration also highlighted NVIDIA RTX Spark and the growing importance of simulation-based learning, humanoid robotics, intelligent automation, and physical artificial intelligence. NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026 provided a glimpse into how artificial intelligence is moving beyond digital applications and into robots that can interact with the real world.

Hugging Face and its Pollen Robotics subsidiary have opened preorders for Microduck, a $399 desktop-sized robot built for experimenting with “physical AI.”  The 25cm robot contains 15 motors, a camera, a depth sensor, two inertial measurement units, and a “beak” that can grasp small objects.  Its open-source software allows developers to train behaviors through reinforcement learning in a physics simulator before transferring them to the real machine.  Microduck can already walk, crouch, follow a laser, grab objects, and recover from many falls.  More than 10,000 units were preordered in its first five days, roughly $4 million! Initial deliveries are targeted before Christmas of this year in North America, Europe, and the UK. Would you buy one?

Do you want this guy rolling around your home? Maybe if it does laundry… Weave Robotics, a San Francisco startup backed by Y Combinator, has launched Isaac 1, a home robot designed to tackle laundry and light tidying. Rather than following the humanoid trend, Isaac 1 uses a wheeled base and extends from three feet to five foot nine depending on the task, with two articulated arms offering an 80-inch vertical reach.  It's built to autonomously locate dirty clothes, manage hampers, and fold garments, though human teleoperators can step in remotely when it gets stuck. And yes, that means someone may occasionally see inside your home through its cameras.  Priced at $7,999 upfront or $449 a month, it undercuts 1X's Neo by more than half. California deliveries begin this fall. #fyp #robot #techtok

I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

🤖 Der Roboter, der sogar die Toilette putzt – das ist tatsächlich Realität! Was zunächst wie ein Zukunftsfilm aussieht, gibt es inzwischen wirklich: Tau Robotics bietet in San Francisco einen humanoiden Reinigungsdienst an. Die Roboter können unter anderem saugen, Oberflächen wischen, Müll wegbringen – und tatsächlich auch Toiletten reinigen. Internationale Medien wie AP und Reuters haben die Roboter bereits bei solchen Arbeiten gezeigt. (YouTube) Allerdings gibt es einen wichtigen Punkt: Der Roboter arbeitet momentan noch nicht vollkommen selbstständig. Ein geschulter Mensch steuert ihn aus der Ferne über die Kameras, während KI das System unterstützt. Die dabei gesammelten Daten sollen helfen, die Roboter Schritt für Schritt autonomer zu machen. (Tau Robotics) Und genau hier könnte es für die Gastronomie irgendwann besonders interessant werden. Wer schon einmal eine stark frequentierte öffentliche Toilette gesehen hat, weiß, wie schwierig und unangenehm die Reinigung sein kann. Ich musste dabei an eine persönliche Erfahrung denken: Als D. bei Co.gearbeitet hat, waren manche Toiletten so stark verschmutzt, dass sogar die Wände betroffen waren. Wenn ein Roboter solche besonders unangenehmen Reinigungsarbeiten irgendwann zuverlässig übernehmen könnte, wäre das tatsächlich ein interessantes Einsatzgebiet. 🦾 Kurz-Steckbrief Unternehmen: Tau Robotics Standort: San Francisco, USA Roboter: humanoide Reinigungsroboter Aktuelle Aufgaben: Saugen, Wischen, Oberflächen reinigen, Müll entfernen und Toiletten reinigen Autonomie: derzeit noch menschlich ferngesteuert bzw. überwacht Preis: 30 US-Dollar pro Roboter und Stunde Status: derzeit nur ausgewählte Kunden / Invite-only (Tau Robotics) 💭 Fazit Vielleicht ist das erst der Anfang einer völlig neuen Art von Reinigung. Heute braucht der Roboter noch einen Menschen im Hintergrund. Morgen könnte er solche Aufgaben möglicherweise selbstständig erledigen. Und wenn die Technik irgendwann zuverlässig funktioniert, könnte gerade die Arbeit, die niemand gerne macht, eine der ersten Aufgaben sein, die Roboter übernehmen. The gap between factory-built robots and DIY projects is getting smaller. Look at these two machines. The top clip shows Galileo, a four-wheeled robot with articulated legs. The robot below is a DIY build made with patched-together parts. I watched the lower clip twice. Its metal frame is exposed and the parts look like they came from different projects. Yet all four wheels move on articulated supports. Pretty impressive for a homemade machine. Motors, controllers, batteries and metal parts are now easier for individual builders to buy and assemble without owning a factory. This short video doesn't prove the DIY robot can match Galileo's performance. We have no figures for payload, accuracy, reliability or lifespan. Factories still do work that's hard to reproduce at home. They machine parts to tight tolerances, inspect assemblies, test safety and produce hundreds or thousands of identical units. But I keep thinking about that bottom robot. Someone assembled a moving four-wheeled machine using improvised parts. That alone would have been a difficult project for most hobbyists years ago. As parts and tools become easier to get, more people can build machines that once seemed out of reach. What happens to assembly factories when complex robots become easier to make at home? Will they focus on precision parts, testing and large-scale production while more assembly moves to small workshops? #Robotics #DIYRobotics #Manufacturing #PhysicalAI
